title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
hook: two old people who waited their whole lives hold the child and say now I can go in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds: the news went to the night shift first, and the angels sang the words of the Gloria.
screen: `GOOD NEWS GOES TO THE OUTSIDERS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to the Temple in Jerusalem, as the law asked of Jewish parents with a firstborn son. They're poor: they bring the offering allowed for families who can't afford a lamb, two birds. It's a busy place, and nobody notices one more young couple. Except two very old people who've been waiting for this their whole lives.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OLD, AT THE TEMPLE.` → `TWO BIRDS: THE POOR FAMILY'S OFFERING.` → `TWO OLD PEOPLE NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Luke says Simeon was a just and devout man, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit had promised him he wouldn't die before he saw the Messiah. How long he'd waited, Luke doesn't say. Years, at least. That day he's moved to go to the Temple. He sees this baby, takes him in his arms, and prays, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." Meaning: I can go now. I've seen it. He calls the child "A light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Then he tells Mary something hard: a sword will pierce her own soul. Joy and warning in one breath. Then comes Anna. Luke calls her a prophetess, very old, widowed after only seven years of marriage, and a widow into her eighties. She never left the Temple, praying and fasting night and day. Decades of waiting in one building. She sees the child, gives thanks, and tells everyone who's been waiting too. Catholics keep this scene close. Simeon's prayer, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first Latin words, is said every night in Night Prayer, the last prayer of the day: now you can let your servant go in peace. The feast is February 2, and because Simeon called the child a light, candles are blessed that day: Candlemas. Remember day fifteen. It's also the fourth joyful mystery of the rosary. All their waiting was pointed somewhere.
screen: `SIMEON: PROMISED HE'D SEE IT.` · `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT.` · `ANNA: DECADES IN THE TEMPLE.` · `CANDLEMAS, FEBRUARY 2.` · then, large: `WAITING IS NOT WASTED.`

segments.voice: Say Simeon's words slowly, here in the Douay-Rheims Bible: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace. Then sit beside what you're still waiting for, healing, a person, a change, an answer, the way Anna sat in the Temple, without pushing it away or grabbing at it. Notice what the waiting has already made of you, the patience, the attention. If you pray, you can offer the waiting to God.
Nunc Dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: the prayer old Simeon prayed, holding the baby he'd waited his whole life to see.
Your line: waiting is not wasted. Go in peace; that's twenty-seven days.

screen: `DAY 27 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MAGI AND THE FLIGHT.`

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, blessing candles at Mass (Candlemas); Simeon's prayer, the Nunc Dimittis, is said every night at Night Prayer.

chat.says: Simeon waited his whole life just to see a baby? Wasn't that time wasted?
options: No, it was pointed somewhere: once he saw the child, he could go in peace.
Yes, but at least seeing the baby healed him so he could live longer.
He wasn't really waiting; he just happened to be at the Temple that day.
chat.meaning: Simeon was promised he'd see the Messiah first. Holding the child, he prayed: now you let your servant go in peace.

Nunc Dimittis.meaning: Simeon's prayer; Latin for 'now you dismiss'

notes: Luke 2:29 and 2:32 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording.
Anna's age: the Greek can mean she was 84, or widowed for 84 years; the voice says 'a widow into her eighties'. Confirm.

Presentation vs purification: the scene combines Mary's purification (Leviticus 12) and the presentation of the firstborn (Exodus 13); simplified as 'as the law asked of Jewish parents with a firstborn son'. Confirm.
The poor family's offering (two birds instead of a lamb, Leviticus 12:8): confirm.
Candlemas and the fourth joyful mystery: confirm.
